newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: From the Hill-Peters asks for more time to settle.
newsitem.headline: From the Hill-Peters asks for more time to settle.

text.p: New Zealand First leader Winston Peters' first news conference as Treasurer on Thursday was a veiled plea to the people and businesses of New Zealand, to give him time to get on top of the job he so keenly sought.

For Peters the Treasurer's job is the jewel in the crown of the coalition deal with National and according to insiders was the circuit-breaker which finally determined whether the eight weeks of negotiation would annoint National or Labour.
It gives him mana in Maoridom as a bulwark against the evitable backlash and an overview of the new government's economic direction.

The impression left with those at the conference was of Peters' new-found public caution; of a man not yet on top of the job wrestling with how he can sell the coalition deal as the means to deliver the economic changes he campaigned for.
His uncertainty may explain why his office has been fobbing off requests for interviews with the excuse Peters is too busy.
From the financial markets' point of view there were some significant uncertainties in what Peters was saying.
On the redrafted policy targets agreement (PTA) he was particularly vague.

The widening of the PTA target from 0-2 percent to 0-3 percent has been easily absorbed by the markets which clearly believe the addition of the sentiment that price stability would be maintained "so that monetary policy can make its maximum contribution to sustainable economic growth, employment and development opportunities within the New Zealand economy" is nothing more than a statement of the worthiness of mother's milk and apple pie.
RBNZ governor Don Brash has indicated he sees no real change to his task from the new wording.
Yet according to Peters the change is more than just flannel, although he evaded saying how.
"You will see from the PTA ... that there is an acceptance of the need for sustainable growth."
He said sustainability and growth were concepts NZ First put central to its coalition talks and that remained the case.

But asked if he expected the Reserve Bank to target anything other than price stability, Peters said: "You'll get no response to that today," adding he would prefer to give a fuller answer to the question in the New Year.
"You have to more carefully examine what were carefully prepared words on behalf of the government. These are early days," Peters said.
Asked if he was indicating changes to the PTA or the Act after further consideration Peters said: "No, I'm flagging caution".

It seems Peters cannot choose between the political damage from admitting the PTA change is purely cosmetic, and the financial damage from saying he expects the governor to change his approach under the new wording.

Several journalists tried unsuccessfully to get Peters to be Whether intentionally or not he left the unstated impression the changes to the PTA may only be interim, with references to it being "early days" and to the PTA being signed off before ministers were sworn in.

Yet it is a tall order to ask the public to accept that, after protracted coalition talks, the government has signed a new contract with the RBNZ governor but is reluctant to comment on the effect it thinks that will have.
While the markets might wear that uncertainty for a while, the honeymoon period will pass and then ... watch this space.

After all, Treasury's briefing to the incoming government -- the reason for Peters' news conference -- was heavy on the need for stability and credibility with warnings of how easily the fiscal gains could be frittered away.
Peters applied the same "wait and see" mantra to his campaign pledges on lowering the dollar, helping exporters and achieving faster growth.

He failed to specify which growth target the government would be aiming for -- the 2.75 percent seen as sustainable by the RBNZ, the 3.5 percent of the Treasury or the 6 percent in NZ First's economic policy. Neither would he say how he would handle the RBNZ leaning against higher growth were it achieved.
The closest he got to his election rhetoric on the need to lower the dollar was the statement: "It would be wrong not be concerned of the affect on exporters."

Asked how he would lower the dollar he said he was not going to make off-the-cuff remarks that would push the dollar around. He may come to realise refusing to comment can create as much uncertainty as off the cuff remarks.
-- Wellington newsroom 64 4 473 4746
